E:\\videos\\olc02\\wt\\vlog\\olc04\\voz\.text: Three dollars of beans, friend. That's what's in this pot. And on Monday it's soup. On Tuesday it's on toast with gravy. On Wednesday it's crisp fried patties with an egg on top. Forty men ate out of this pot for three days and not one of them ever knew it was the same pot. And I know what happens in most houses. Somebody cooks a big pot of beans on Sunday. Everybody eats it Sunday night. They eat it again Monday night, and by Tuesday nobody wants to look at it. The rest goes in the back of the refrigerator, and on Saturday it goes in the trash. And the bag of beans sits in the cupboard for a year after that, because beans are boring. Beans are not boring. Eating the same thing three nights in a row is boring, and that's not the beans' fault, and it isn't yours either. Nobody ever showed you that one pot of beans is not one supper. It's the start of five, you

So tonight I'm going to show you exactly how I made one pot feed my camp for three days. How to cook the pot right the first time, so the beans are creamy and not hard or split. And then the three suppers that come out of it, each one different enough that nobody at your table will complain. And I priced it all at the store this week. One pound of dry pinto beans and a piece of salt pork, about three dollars. That pot, with a few things you already have, makes about 15 plates over three days. Twenty cents a bean's a plate, friend. You can't buy anything cheaper that fills you up like this. And the third supper, the bean patties, is the one people never believe until they taste it. Big Swede called them lager's hamburgers. You know me. I'm Olay.

I cooked in the logging camps up in northern Minnesota in a log cook shack with a wood range and a bean pot so big I needed both arms and a strong back to lift it. My mother taught me first in a little farmhouse kitchen with a blue enamel coffee pot that never left the back of the stove. Quick, while I have you, the no-soap bean method I'm about to show you is on page 7 of my cookbook and 32 ways to stretch a $2 bag of beans are in my little book called Oli's Bean Pot. The card with the square code is right here on the table. Point your phone at it and it takes you straight there. Now to the stove. Let me tell you where this started. My first winter as head cook, the boss came into the cook shack with the ledger under his arm and told me I was spending too much on meat. Cut it by a third, Oli, or he'd find a cook who could. 40 men and a third less meat.

I went out behind the cook shack and stood in the snow for a while, I'll tell you that. And then the old cook from the camp across the lake, a Finn named I know, who'd been cooking since before I was born, came over on snowshoes to borrow some yeast. I told him my trouble. He laughed at me. He said, oh, you're cooking beans like a farmer. One pot, one supper. A camp cook cooks one pot and gets three suppers out of it. Then he showed me, and I've done it his way ever since. First, why beans in a logging camp? Because they came in by the hundred-pound sack in the fall. They never spoiled, they didn't need ice, and they didn't freeze on the sled. Fresh meat was expensive, and half the winter we didn't have any. Beans and a little salt pork, that was the backbone of every camp kitchen I ever worked in. And here's the arithmetic most people never do.

A one-pound bag of dry pintos at the store is about $1.80. Cooked, it makes about six cups. A can of beans, one and a half cups, is about $1.25. So the bag gives you four cans worth of beans for the price of a can and a half. Cook a bag every week for a year and that's hundreds of dollars left in your pocket from one thing. Now the pot. Part one is picking. Pour your beans out on a sheet pan and look at them. you'll find little stones, a cloud of dirt, a few shriveled or broken beans. Pick them out. In the camp, the cookie did this every morning, and once Lars found a stone the size of a pea that would have broken somebody's tooth. Then rinse them in a colander. And now here's the thing everybody argues about. You do not need to soak them overnight. Soaking saves you 20 or 30 minutes of simmer. That's all. If you forgot to soak them, you lost nothing.

And if you did soak them, pour off that water and use fresh. Part 2. Salt goes in at the start. Your grandmother probably told you salt makes beans hard. It doesn't. That's an old tale that got passed down. One tablespoon of kosher salt for a pound of beans right in the pot at the beginning. The salt seasons them all the way to the middle and keeps the skins tender. Now the pork. Cut a quarter pound of salt pork or three or four strips of thick bacon into pieces and put them in with the beans. Add an onion cut in half and a bay leaf if you have one. Cover everything with water about two inches over the top of the beans. Part 3. A hard boil. Ten full minutes. Bring the pot up to a rolling boil and hold it there. Don't skip this. It's the safety step for red kidney beans especially, and it's good practice for any dry bean.

A slow cooker alone never gets hot enough to do it, so even if you finish in a slow cooker, boil them on the stove first. And part four, the whisper. After those ten minutes, turn the heat down until only a bubble or two breaks the surface and crack the lid. That's what I mean by a whisper. The hard boil after the first ten minutes splits the skins and turns the beans to mush. A whisper cooks them creamy and whole. Pean toast take about an hour and a half to two hours like that. And here's how you know they're done. The old camp test. Take a spoonful, blow on it. If the skins wrinkle and peel back, they're close. Then bite five beans. All five should be creamy all the way through. If one is chalky, give it 15 more minutes. One more roux, vinegar, tomatoes, molasses, anything sour or sweet, goes in last, only when the beans are already soft. Acid keeps beans hard.

That's why some people cook baked beans for six hours and they're still crunchy. They put the tomato in too early. So that's your pot. On the first night, you serve them just like that. Pot beans with the salt pork, in a bowl with the broth, and a piece of cornbread on the side. And here's the first rule of the three-day pot. Don't serve the whole thing. Take out what you need for supper and put the rest away right. Cool it fast. Next never leave the big pot sitting on the stove overnight. Spread the beans out in shallow containers so they cool within two hours, then into the refrigerator in their broth. That broth is gold, friend. Don't you dare pour it down the drain. Cooked beans keep four or five days that way. Now day one, Monday, soup, and this one takes five minutes.

Two cups of leftover beans, a cup and a half of the bean broth, two slices of bacon, half an onion, half a teaspoon of paprika, salt, pepper, and a splash of vinegar. Fry the bacon in a small pot until it's crisp. Take half of it out for the top. Cook the onion in that fat four minutes. Add the paprika. Then the beans and the broth go in. Bring it to a simmer and mash it right in the pot with a potato masher until it's thick. Then the vinegar, just a splash, at the end. That's the secret. Bean soup without a little sour at the end, tastes flat, like something's missing, and nobody can tell you what. A splash of vinegar, and suddenly it tastes finished. About 50 cents a bowl. Tarvo didn't like beans. He told me that every single week. And every Monday, he had two bowls of this soup, because it didn't look like beans, and it didn't taste like sundae,

That's the whole trick of the three-day pot. Change the shape and change the taste, and it's a new supper. Day two, Tuesday. Beans on toast with bean broth gravy. And this is a camp cook's secret, that broth you saved. It makes a gravy that tastes like it took all afternoon. Three tablespoons of bacon fat or butter in a skillet. Three tablespoons of flour. Stir it two or three minutes until it smells a little nutty and turns light brown. Then whisk in two cups of the bean broth, slowly, a little at a time, so it doesn't lump. Simmer five minutes until it coats a spoon. Salt and a lot of black pepper. Now here's why it works. The bean broth already has body from the starch of the beans, so it needs less flour than any other gravy, and it never tastes like paste. Put a couple cups of beans into that gravy to warm through, and ladle it over thick slices of toast.

or over biscuits if you're feeling generous. In the camp we used yesterday's bread, toasted on top of the wood range, right on the iron. Halver used to ask for the burned pieces. He said the black parts were the best. That gravy cost about ten cents a serving, friend. The toast cost more than the gravy. And day three, Wednesday, the bean patties, lagers, hamburgers, two cups of beans, half a cup of breadcrumbs or crushed crackers, 1 egg, half an onion grated, a teaspoon of cumin if you have it, half a teaspoon of salt, a handful of grated cheese if there is some, and a few tablespoons of fat for frying. Now, the reason most bean patties fall apart in the pan is water, so here's the trick. Drain the beans well and pat them dry on a towel before you mash them. Wet beans are why bean cakes fall apart. Dry beans hold. Mash half of the beans to a paste and leave the other half whole.

That way they hold together and still have something to bite. Mix in the crumbs, the egg, the onion, the cumin, the salt, then let it sit 10 minutes so the crumbs soak up what's left of the moisture. Shape them into patties about half an inch thick and fry them in hot fat over medium, 4 minutes a side, until a dark crust forms. Don't move them before then. Put a fried egg on top or put them in a bun with a slice of onion, about 40 cents a serving. the first time i made these big swede picked one up with his fingers looked at it bit it and said ole this is a hamburger i said no it's beans he said don't tell anybody and for the rest of that winter wednesday was hamburger night and nobody told anybody and if there's still some left on thursday and with a big pot there often is you have more choices

Fry the beans with leftover potatoes and an onion in a skillet. Press it flat, let it get a crust, and crack eggs on top. That's bean and potato hash. Or mash a cup of beans smooth into your cornbread batter. Nobody will know, and the cornbread stays moist for three days. And one more. For the lunch pail, a cup of cold beans, a little chopped onion, a spoon of vinegar, and a spoon of oil, salt and pepper. that's a bean salad and it's better the next day the men carried it out to the cut in their tin pails with a piece of bread and it never froze solid the way the meat sandwiches did a lunch for pennies so you see friend the pot is not the supper the pot is the pantry you cook it once on sunday and then all week the pot cooks for you that's what he no meant and it's the reason a Camp Cook could feed 40 men on what a farmer spent feeding his family. And one last thing.

If you have a little bean broth left at the very end of the week and no beans, don't pour it out. Warm it in a cup with a pinch of salt and drink it. The men in my camp did that in the morning before they went out in the cold. A tin cup of hot bean broth. It warms you right through. Waste nothing, friend. Not even the water the beans were cooked in. I'll tell you about the worst bean week I ever had. It was early in my first winter as head cook. The supply sled was late, the snow was up past the windows, and all I had left in the cellar was a sack of pintos, a slab of salt pork, onions and flour, forty men, and nothing but beans for six days. I thought they'd hang me from the cook-shack door. So I did what I'm showing you today. Monday was soup, Tuesday was gravy on toast, Wednesday was patties, Thursday I baked them with a little molasses and mustard.

Friday was bean and onion pie with a biscuit crust, and Saturday Arvid came in, sat down and said, Oh, what kind of meat is this? It was beans, friend, the same beans as Monday. Nobody knew. That week taught me the most important thing I ever learned in a kitchen. Men don't get tired of beans. They get tired of the same plate. Change the shape, change the texture, change what's around it, and the same pot feeds you happy all week long. Now if your beans come out wrong, it isn't you. If they're still hard after two hours, they're old beans, more than a year on the shelf, or something sour went in too early. If the skin's split and they're mushy, the boil was too hard after the first ten minutes. If the patties fall apart, the beans were wet. And if the soup tastes flat, it needs the vinegar. Let me do the arithmetic for you. One pound of dry pintos, about a dollar eighty.

a quarter pound of salt pork or a few strips of bacon, about $1.20, $3 for the pot. Add an onion, some flour, a couple eggs, some bread you already have, and you've got Sunday supper and three more suppers out of it. The same beans out of cans would cost you about $7 before you even added anything, and a side of beans at the drive-thru is a few dollars for a little paper cup, one pot, four suppers, maybe 15 plates, and nobody at your table complaining about beans. So here's the whole thing. Pick and rinse, no soap needed, salt at the start, 10 minutes of hard boil, then a whisper, sour things last, cool it fast and save the broth, Monday soup with a splash of vinegar, Tuesday gravy on toast, Wednesday patties, with the beans dried first. Here's your homework, friend, just two things.

This Sunday, put the salt in at the start and keep the pot at a whisper and don't pour the bean broth down the drain. Do only that and you'll already cook better beans than most restaurants. And tell me in the comments, what did your family do with the leftover beans? Some families fried them, some put them in soup, some ate them cold on bread. I want to know what your grandmother did with the last of the pot. The bean method is on page 7 of my cookbook, and all 32 ways to stretch a bag of beans are in Ole's Bean Pot. The card is right there on the table. Next time I'll tell you about the day I found my old camp skillet rusted in a barn, 40 years after I lost it, and how I brought it back. Keep the pot going, friend. I'll see you at the table.
